<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-grounded cases without fake citations, but PRO navigated the pressure exchange more decisively. PRO's pressure questions forced CON to either name a non-fine tool that reaches the resourced-but-unwilling refuser or admit acceptance of some fine design; CON's answer ("I'd accept exactly PRO's amended version... a genuine last-resort penalty for documented bad-faith refusal") was a real concession that undercut CON's blanket "fines are the wrong lever" thesis, even though CON tried to caveat it as not the literal motion. PRO then used the motion's own words ("repeatedly," "meaningful") to argue proportionality and warning-based process are natural readings rather than invented add-ons, and deployed a self-selection argument (capacity-poor orgs who engage never reach the fine stage) that CON never fully dismantled in the closing — CON reasserted the capacity-poor statistic but didn't re-engage the self-selection mechanism head-on. CON's strongest material (big firms absorbing fines, compliance-theater incentives, concrete alternative toolkit) remained live and rhetorically sharp, but its central "blunt instrument" framing was weakened by CON's own concession under pressure, and PRO's closing capitalized on that (even if slightly overstating it as full concession of the whole motion). This makes PRO's path to victory clearer and more resilient by the end of the exchange.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure question forcing CON to name a tool reaching the "willful refuser," answered in CON's Rebuttal 2 with an explicit acceptance of "a genuine last-resort penalty for documented bad-faith refusal" — a concession PRO then leveraged throughout the rest of the debate to argue CON had effectively conceded the core mechanism the motion describes.</best_rebuttal>
